cases.description: Two members of one JSON object named a fail parse at the second; JSON.parse and Python's json keep the last one silently.
A duplicate inside a nested object is an error at that object's member, even when both values are equal.
"\u0061" names the same member as "a", since I-JSON compares names after processing escapes (RFC 7493, section 2.3); a check on the raw text misses it.
A name with a precomposed é (NFC) and one with e and a combining acute accent (NFD) are different names, since strings are not normalized, so the record has two members.
A string in NFD keeps its combining accent in the value view; a reader that normalizes to NFC gives a different string.
"\ud83d\ude00" is a surrogate pair, the way JSON escapes a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (RFC 8259, section 7), so it is the one character U+1F600 and valid.
"\ud800" is a high surrogate with no low surrogate after it, which is not valid Unicode; every JSON parser surveyed except serde_json accepts it (Appendix B).
"\uDEAD", RFC 7493's own example, is a low surrogate with no high surrogate before it.
An unpaired surrogate between other characters of a string in an array is an error at that string.
A record with an unpaired surrogate and a duplicate member reports both, not only the first (§9.2).
A YAML mapping with the key a twice fails parse at the second; PyYAML keeps the last one silently (parser survey, section 4.2).
The plain key a and the quoted key "a" are the same string, so they are duplicates.
A duplicate key in a flow mapping is an error at that mapping's member.

The YAML escape \ud800 in a double-quoted scalar gives an unpaired surrogate, which every reader in the columns of the parser survey's section 4.2 accepts; libyaml's scanner, which Psych and PyYAML's CSafeLoader use, rejects it, and a reader built on libyaml must still report unpaired-surrogate, not syntax-error.
The 32-bit YAML escape \U0000DC00 (YAML 1.2.2, section 5.7) names a lone low surrogate too, and a reader built on libyaml, whose scanner rejects it, must report unpaired-surrogate, not syntax-error.
Front matter is a YAML mapping, so a key repeated in it is a duplicate-member error at the second, a structural error rather than the duplicate-key of §5.7.
A name given three times is reported once for each occurrence after the first (Appendix D), so the record has two duplicate-member issues at /a.
A YAML key given three times gives two duplicate-member issues, one per occurrence after the first (Appendix D).
"\udc00\ud800" is a low surrogate followed by a high one, so neither is part of a pair; unpaired-surrogate is reported once per string, however many it holds (Appendix D).
An unpaired surrogate in a member name is reported at the object that holds the member (Appendix D), since the member's own exact path would hold the lone surrogate.
Noncharacters are valid (§4.1), where I-JSON forbids them (RFC 7493, section 2.1): U+FFFF, U+FDD0 and U+1FFFE, the last written as a surrogate pair, are read as written.
Raw noncharacters U+FFFF and U+FDD0 in a JSON file are valid, as escaped ones are.

Two \u escapes that form a surrogate pair read as the one character U+1F600, as in JSON (§4.1). YAML 1.2.2 calls \u a 16-bit escape and does not say that two combine; the yaml package (2.9.1) combines them, and a reader that does not must combine them itself.
U+FFFE is outside YAML's character set, so YAML writes it as an escape, "\uFFFE", which reads as the noncharacter, a valid string (§4.1).
U+FDD0 is a noncharacter inside YAML's character set (c-printable includes xE000 to xFFFD), so it may appear raw in a plain scalar.
A raw U+FFFE is outside YAML's character set (YAML 1.2.2, section 5.1), so the file is a YAML syntax error, reported at the root (§4.1); the yaml package (2.9.1) accepts it.
Front matter is YAML, so a raw U+FFFE in it is a syntax error too, which Appendix D attaches to the record, at its root.
